inline_comments.comment: The literal `11` is a magic number that represents `THEME_COLOR_LIMIT - 1`. `styles.ts` loops `for (let i = 0; i < THEME_COLOR_LIMIT; i++)` and emits `section-${i - 1}`, so with `THEME_COLOR_LIMIT = 12` the valid child section classes are `section-0` through `section-10` — 11 classes. This implicit coupling means that if `THEME_COLOR_LIMIT` is ever incremented in `theme-base.js` (e.g. to add a new palette colour), this modulo will silently under-utilise the new class and the two values will drift apart without any compile-time or test-time signal. Consider either extracting a named constant (e.g. `const NUM_SECTION_STYLES = 11`) with a comment explaining its origin, or importing / referencing `THEME_COLOR_LIMIT` directly so the relationship is explicit.

`Array.prototype.find` returns `T | undefined`, and the `as MindmapLayoutNode` cast does not eliminate that possibility — it merely suppresses the TypeScript error. If any of these six `find` calls returns `undefined` (e.g. because `getData()` transforms the label, or because of a future regression), the failure will surface as a cryptic "Cannot read properties of undefined" on the subsequent `.section` or `.cssClasses` access, with no indication of which node was missing. Add `expect(childN).toBeDefined()` (or `toBeTruthy()`) immediately after each `find` so that a missing node produces a clear, actionable failure message. This applies to all six variable declarations on lines 308–313.

general_comments.comment: The new test validates the first child (index 0 → section 0), the eleventh child (index 10 → section 10), and children 12–15 (the wrap-around group), but skips children 2–10 entirely. While the logic is simple, an off-by-one in the `% 11` expression or in how `entries()` starts its index would not be caught for the middle range. Adding at least one mid-range assertion (e.g. `expect(child6.section).toBe(5)`) would give stronger assurance that sections 1–9 are also assigned correctly.
